AUTOMATIC TEMPORARY RESTRAINING ORDERS (ATROS) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Automatic Temporary Restraining Orders (ATROS) Information Sheet concerns a proceeding for dissolution of marriage between Jordan Alex Lee, as petitioner, and Taylor Morgan, as respondent, filed or to be filed in the California superior court for Alameda County. It describes the temporary restraining orders that California Family Code section 2040 requires be included in the summons for such a proceeding — restraining orders that attach automatically upon the filing of the petition and the issuance of the summons, without either party separately requesting them and without a judge separately signing a further order. It is not itself a summons, petition, or restraining order, and completing it does not create, modify, or terminate any restraining order affecting Jordan Alex Lee or Taylor Morgan. Only the summons issued in an actual proceeding, applying the statute described here, does that.

ATROS ATTACH AUTOMATICALLY TO THE SUMMONS IN A DISSOLUTION, NULLITY, OR LEGAL SEPARATION PROCEEDING
California Family Code section 2040(a) states that, in addition to the contents required by Code of Civil Procedure section 412.20, the summons in a covered proceeding "shall contain a temporary restraining order" — the orders are a required part of the summons itself, not a separate order a party must ask a judge to sign. Family Code section 231 states that this restraining-order framework applies to a summons issued under Family Code section 2040, which governs a proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties, and separately to a summons issued under Family Code section 7700, which governs a proceeding under the Uniform Parentage Act. Because the restraining orders described in this document are a mandatory component of the summons in these proceedings, they bind both the party who filed the petition and the other party without either party filing a separate request or declaration of abuse — unlike a domestic violence restraining order, which a party must actively request based on alleged abuse.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "In addition to the contents required by Section 412.20 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the summons shall contain a temporary restraining order:"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a) (California Legislative Information text), the summons must contain the temporary restraining order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  "This part applies to a temporary restraining order in a summons issued under any of the following provisions: (a) Section 2040 (proceeding for dissolution of marriage, for nullity of marriage, or for legal separation of the parties)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 231 (California Legislative Information text), scope: applies to summonses under section 2040 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=231.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two different, separately codified Family Code sections — section 2040(a) (the operative-text requirement that the summons contain the restraining order) and section 231 (the scope provision listing which types of summons the restraining-order framework applies to) — rather than multiple subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies here. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how California structures its automatic restraining-order process for dissolution, nullity, and legal-separation proceedings — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific petitioner's or respondent's proceeding, or that an equivalent automatic mechanism exists in any other state. This document addresses only the restraining orders under Family Code section 2040 (the dissolution/nullity/legal-separation branch of section 231); it does not address the separate restraining orders under Family Code section 7700 for Uniform Parentage Act proceedings, which this document's research did not independently verify.

WHEN ATROS TAKE EFFECT FOR THE PETITIONER AND THE RESPONDENT, HOW LONG THEY LAST, AND HOW THEY ARE ENFORCED
California Family Code section 233(a) states that the temporary restraining order in the summons takes effect against a party at a different moment depending on which party that is: it is in effect against the petitioner upon the filing of the petition and issuance of the summons, and it is in effect against the respondent upon personal service of the petition and summons on the respondent, or upon the respondent's waiver and acceptance of service. Once in effect against a given party, the order remains in effect against that party until final judgment is entered, the petition is dismissed, or the court orders otherwise. Section 233(b) states that the order is enforceable anywhere in the state, but that a local law enforcement agency need not enforce it unless that agency has received mailed notice of the order, has otherwise received a copy of it, or has been shown a copy by the officer enforcing it. Section 233(c) states that a willful and knowing violation of the child-removal order is punishable under Penal Code section 278.5, and that a willful and knowing violation of any of the other orders in the summons is punishable under Penal Code section 273.6.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) Upon filing the petition and issuance of the summons and upon personal service of the petition and summons on the respondent or upon waiver and acceptance of service by the respondent, the temporary restraining order under this part shall be in effect against the parties until the final judgment is entered or the petition is dismissed, or until further order of the court. (b) The temporary restraining order is enforceable in any place in this state, but is not enforceable by a law enforcement agency of a political subdivision unless that law enforcement agency has received mailed notice of the order or has otherwise received a copy of the order or the officer enforcing the order has been shown a copy of the order. (c) A willful and knowing violation of the order included in the summons by removing a child from the state without the written consent of the other party or an order of the court is punishable as provided in Section 278.5 of the Penal Code. A willful and knowing violation of any of the other orders included in the summons is punishable as provided in Section 273.6 of the Penal Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 233(a)–(c) (California Legislative Information text), effective dates by party, duration, enforceability, and violation consequences (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=233.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from the three subdivisions — (a), (b), and (c) — of a single Family Code section, section 233, so this is a single-section citation rather than independent corroboration from separate sections; the subdivisions are quoted together because they form one continuous statutory paragraph on timing, duration, and enforcement. Section 233 sits in Family Code Division 2 (General Provisions), not in Division 6 alongside section 2040 itself; this document treats it as governing the section 2040 restraining orders addressed here because Family Code section 231 (quoted in a separate clause of this document) expressly states that section 233's framework applies to a summons issued under section 2040. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own timing and enforcement rules for this restraining order — not a claim about any other state's procedure, and not a determination that a specific violation in a specific case meets the statutory standard for a willful and knowing violation; that determination belongs to a court applying the statute and the Penal Code sections it references to particular facts.

RESTRAINT ON TRANSFERRING OR ENCUMBERING PROPERTY, AND ITS STATED EXCEPTIONS
California Family Code section 2040(a)(2)(A) restrains both parties from transferring, encumbering, hypothecating, concealing, or otherwise disposing of any real or personal property — whether community, quasi-community, or separate — without the other party's written consent or a court order. The statute states its own exceptions on the face of that same restraint: a transfer in the usual course of business, and a transfer for the necessities of life. The same provision also requires each party to notify the other of a proposed extraordinary expenditure at least five business days before incurring it, and to account to the court for extraordinary expenditures made after service of the summons. Section 2040(a)(2)(B) states a further, separate exception: the restraining order does not preclude a party from using community property, quasi-community property, or the party's own separate property to pay reasonable attorney's fees and costs to retain counsel in the proceeding, though a party who uses community or quasi-community property for that purpose must account to the community for its use, and a party who uses property later determined to be the other party's separate property must account to that other party for its use.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Restraining both parties from transferring, encumbering, hypothecating, concealing, or in any way disposing of, any property, real or personal, whether community, quasi-community, or separate, without the written consent of the other party or an order of the court, except in the usual course of business or for the necessities of life, and requiring each party to notify the other party of proposed extraordinary expenditures at least five business days before incurring those expenditures and to account to the court for all extraordinary expenditures made after service of the summons on that party."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), property-transfer restraint and its exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  "the restraining order shall not preclude a party from using community property, quasi-community property, or the party’s own separate property to pay reasonable attorney’s fees and costs in order to retain legal counsel in the proceeding."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), exception for paying attorney's fees and costs (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from subparagraphs (A) and (B) of a single paragraph — Family Code section 2040(a)(2) — of a single section, so this is a single-section citation, not independent corroboration from separate statutes. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own property-transfer restraint and its stated exceptions — not a claim about any other state's equivalent restraining-order process. Whether a specific transaction falls within "the usual course of business," qualifies as a necessity of life, or was made with adequate written consent is a factual and legal determination this clause does not make for any individual case.

RESTRAINT ON REMOVING A MINOR CHILD FROM THE STATE OR APPLYING FOR A PASSPORT
California Family Code section 2040(a)(1) restrains both parties from removing a minor child of the parties from the state, and from applying for a new or replacement passport for that child, without either the other party's prior written consent or a court order. As with the property restraint described elsewhere in this document, the statute states the exceptions — prior written consent or a court order — on the face of the restraint itself, rather than leaving them to be inferred.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Restraining both parties from removing the minor child or children of the parties, if any, from the state, or from applying for a new or replacement passport for the minor child or children, without the prior written consent of the other party or an order of the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), restraint on removing a minor child from the state or applying for a passport (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own restriction on removing a child from the state or seeking a passport during a covered proceeding — not a claim about any other state's law, and not a determination of whether a specific planned trip or passport application in a specific case would violate this restraint or fall within its consent or court-order exception. Whether a particular consent was sufficiently "written" and given by the party with authority to give it is a factual question this clause does not resolve.

RESTRAINT ON CANCELING INSURANCE COVERAGE OR CHANGING BENEFICIARIES
California Family Code section 2040(a)(3), in the version of the statute operative from January 1, 2026 through January 1, 2027, restrains both parties from cashing, borrowing against, canceling, transferring, disposing of, or changing the beneficiaries of any insurance or other coverage — including life, health, automobile, and disability coverage — held for the benefit of the parties or their child or children for whom support may be ordered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Restraining both parties from cashing, borrowing against, canceling, transferring, disposing of, or changing the beneficiaries of insurance or other coverage, including life, health, automobile, and disability, held for the benefit of the parties and their child or children for whom support may be ordered."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text; operative Jan. 1, 2026 – Jan. 1, 2027), restraint on insurance/coverage changes and beneficiary designations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  "Restraining both parties from cashing, borrowing against, canceling, allowing to lapse for nonpayment of premiums, failing to renew, transferring, disposing of, or changing the beneficiaries of insurance or other coverage, including life, health, automobile, and disability, held for the benefit of the parties and their child or children for whom support may be ordered."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text; operative Jan. 1, 2027), same restraint, as amended to add lapse/nonrenewal language, effective Jan. 1, 2027 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own restraint on insurance and coverage changes during a covered proceeding — not a claim about any other state's law. Family Code section 2040 was amended by the same 2025 enactment (Stats. 2025, Ch. 48) in two operative-date phases: the text quoted above is Sec. 1 of that chapter, operative January 1, 2026 through January 1, 2027 (the version in effect as of this clause's checked date), and Sec. 2 of the same chapter adds further language to this identical paragraph — "allowing to lapse for nonpayment of premiums, failing to renew" — becoming operative January 1, 2027. Both citations below are two operative-date versions of the same enacted chapter and the same statutory paragraph, not independent corroboration from separate sources; the second is included only to disclose the change already fixed to take effect, not as evidence beyond what the first citation already establishes.

RESTRAINT ON NONPROBATE TRANSFERS, AND WHAT ATROS DO NOT RESTRAIN
California Family Code section 2040(a)(4) restrains both parties from creating or modifying a nonprobate transfer — an instrument other than a will that transfers property on death, such as a revocable trust, a pay-on-death account, or a transfer-on-death deed — in a manner that affects the disposition of the property it covers, without the other party's written consent or a court order. Section 2040(b) then states five things the statute does not restrain: creating, modifying, or revoking a will; revoking a nonprobate transfer such as a revocable trust according to its own terms, provided notice of the change is filed and served on the other party before the change takes effect; eliminating a right of survivorship to property, on the same filed-and-served-notice condition; creating an unfunded revocable or irrevocable trust; and filing a disclaimer under Probate Code Part 8 (commencing with section 260).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Restraining both parties from creating a nonprobate transfer or modifying a nonprobate transfer in a manner that affects the disposition of property subject to the transfer, without the written consent of the other party or an order of the court."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), restraint on creating or modifying a nonprobate transfer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  "This section does not restrain any of the following: (1) Creation, modification, or revocation of a will. (2) Revocation of a nonprobate transfer, including a revocable trust, pursuant to the instrument, provided that notice of the change is filed and served on the other party before the change takes effect. (3) Elimination of a right of survivorship to property, provided that notice of the change is filed and served on the other party before the change takes effect. (4) Creation of an unfunded revocable or irrevocable trust. (5) Execution and filing of a disclaimer pursuant to Part 8 (commencing with Section 260) of Division 2 of the Probate Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 2040(b) (California Legislative Information text), five things ATROS do not restrain (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=2040.)
  Known gap: This clause is drawn from subdivisions (a)(4) and (b) of a single Family Code section, section 2040, so this is a single-section citation, not independent corroboration from separate statutes. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's own nonprobate-transfer restraint and its stated exceptions — not a claim about any other state's law. This clause does not restate section 2040(d)'s statutory definition of "nonprobate transfer" in full, or the related carve-out in section 2040(d)(2) for a beneficiary designation in an insurance policy (which this document's insurance-restraint clause addresses separately); whether a specific instrument qualifies as a nonprobate transfer, or whether a specific notice was timely "filed and served" before a change took effect, is a factual and legal determination this clause does not make for any individual case.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________

This clause does not restate section 2040(d)'s statutory definition of "nonprobate transfer" in full, or the related carve-out in section 2040(d)(2) for a beneficiary designation in an insurance policy (which this document's insurance-restraint clause addresses separately); whether a specific instrument qualifies as a nonprobate transfer, or whether a specific notice was timely "filed and served" before a change took effect, is a factual and legal determination this clause does not make for any individual case.

I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Oakland, California.

[This information sheet is prepared for background use alongside an actual petition and summons for dissolution of marriage filed with the California superior court for Alameda County. It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition or summons, and it does not create, modify, or terminate any restraining order affecting Jordan Alex Lee or Taylor Morgan; only a summons issued in an actual proceeding, applying Family Code section 2040 and the related sections it cross-references, does that.]
